title: Макс в роли гостя и гордость Насти  (Max Poses as a Guest and Nastya's Pride)

segments.t: Determined to get an audience with Viktor Petrovich, Max sits down at a table in the dining room and has a waiter summon the head chef to speak with a guest—only to get thrown out again. Meanwhile, Nastya asks Vika to stop helping Kostya plan his proposal.
А что, Елена Павловна?
Я принимаю условия вашей игры.
Шеф, вас там гость зовет.
Здравствуйте, вы хотели меня видеть.
Здравствуйте, Никита Петрович.
Хотя, помните, у вас работал молодой повар?
Быстро вон из ресторана.
Ну-ну, стой.
Химчистку мы вам оплатим.
Я поняла, Костя.
Настя, ты не могла бы выйти?
Виктория Сергеевна, вы не должны помогать Косте.
Он мужчина и сам должен сделать мне предложение.
Now let's go back through the conversation line by line.
А что, Елена Павловна?
'Well, how about that, Elena Pavlovna?' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'and' and finishing on 'Pavlovna'. Vika answers right away.
Я принимаю условия вашей игры.
'I accept the terms of your little game.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'I' and finishing on 'games'.
Шеф, вас там гость зовет.
'Chef, a guest out in the dining room is asking for you.' Kostya anchors the line on 'chef', while 'calls' completes the thought.
Здравствуйте, вы хотели меня видеть.
'Hello, you wanted to see me?' Chef Viktor chooses the respectful plural 'you' alongside 'to see' to keep a polite distance. Vika answers right away.
Здравствуйте, Никита Петрович.
'Hello there, Viktor Petrovich.' Notice how Russian expresses 'hello' and 'Petrovich' with crisp inflection rather than helper words.
Хотя, помните, у вас работал молодой повар?
'By the way, do you remember a young cook who used to work for you?' Kostya anchors the line on 'at least', while 'chef' completes the thought.
Быстро вон из ресторана.
'Get out of this restaurant right now.' In Russian, the idea of 'quickly' flows naturally into 'restaurant' without extra filler words. Vika answers right away.
Ну-ну, стой.
'Hold on, wait a second.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'yeah' before landing on 'stop'.
Химчистку мы вам оплатим.
'We will gladly pay for your dry cleaning.' Here the Russian phrasing highlights 'dry cleaner’s' before landing on 'to pay'.
Я поняла, Костя.
'I understand, Kostya.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'I' and finishing on 'Kostya'. Vika answers right away.
Настя, ты не могла бы выйти?
'Nastya, could you step out for a moment?' In Russian, the idea of 'Nastya' flows naturally into 'to marry' without extra filler words.
Виктория Сергеевна, вы не должны помогать Косте.
'Viktoriya Sergeyevna, you must not help Kostya with this.' Spoken Russian keeps this brisk, leaning on 'Viktoriya' and finishing on 'Kostya'.
Он мужчина и сам должен сделать мне предложение.

'He is a man and must propose to me on his own.' Notice how Russian expresses 'he' and 'offer' with crisp inflection rather than helper words. Alright, let's hear the whole conversation once more from start to finish.
